newsitem.title: JAPAN: FOCUS-Japan tankan shows mixed mood, no rate shift.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Japan tankan shows mixed mood, no rate shift.

text.p: A key central bank survey released on Wednesday showed some improvement in the mood of corporate Japan but also highlighted insecurity about the future, leaving policymakers little room to tighten credit.

The Bank of Japan's quarterly "tankan" revealed a growing divide in business confidence between big manufacturers, which were more positive than in the last survey, and other sectors, which were surprisingly downcast.

Analysts said the results of the corporate survey, reflecting fears that higher taxes will stall Japan's tentative economic recovery, were not bright enough to spur the Bank of Japan to lift interest rates from their rock-bottom levels.

The key index measuring the mood of major manufacturers improved to plus two in March from minus three in the previous survey last November, the first positive reading since November 1991 and at the higher end of economists' expectations.
But this contrasted sharply with the mood among non-manufacturers, whose index plunged beyond most expectations to minus six from zero in November.

The indices, based on a questionnaire circulated to companies, represent the percentage of firms which see business conditions as favourable minus those which see conditions as unfavourable. The higher the number, the better the outlook.
"The gap between industries has risen to the fore. Large manufacturers are doing very well but everybody else isn't," said Hisashi Yamada, an economist at the Japan Research Institute.
"Basically Japan's economic pie is not growing -- the stronger are grabbing a bigger piece of the pie and weaker ones are losing out," he said.
Indices measuring how firms expect to feel in June, when the next tankan is conducted, pointed to a darkening mood.
For June, the manufacturing index was minus one -- dipping back into negative territory -- while the non-manufacturers' index was minus seven.

The Bank of Japan said a weaker yen had helped exports, providing a better environment for manufacturers, but that a peaking out of public works spending and housing investment had dampened sentiment among non-manufacturers.
But the bank said although there would be some fallout from the sales tax rise which took effect on April 1, the economy was unlikely to slip off its recovery track.
"Although there are some effects seen from the consumption tax hike, overall it (the economy) is firm," said Masayuki Matsushima, director of the central bank's Research and Statistics Department.

Economists said that while big manufacturers had gone through a solid restructuring phase, many non-manufacturing sectors were still coddled in a protectionist environment and lacked a competitive edge.

Analysts also said the central bank would be unlikely to hazard a rate rise with the non-manufacturing sector so weak. "This is a sign that we are likely to see a stable (discount rate) for several months to come, probably for many months to come," said Jane Berryman, a senior analyst at Technical Data.
The Bank of Japan has kept the key interest rate at a record low of 0.5 percent since September 1995 in a bid to kick the economy out of four-and-a-half years of recession.

Some also said the underlying tone of the survey was stronger than at first glance, pointing to increased capital spending. Both large manufacturers and non-manufacturers expected a rise of 2.7 percent in capital spending for the next business year. "That's a huge improvement on what they normally forecast at this time of the year," said one economist.
